title: How Spec-Driven Development Shaped My New Way of Engineering
body_markdown:
Before adopting spec-driven development (SDD), I spent a lot of my time renegotiating with AI agents before we reached a plan I was happy with. Worse, without persisted artifacts or structured task tracking, agents would routinely suffer context window decay.


Illustration of a developer looking overwhelmed while surrounded by floating panels of code.


Without SDD, my AI-assisted work wasn’t leaving durable records of what had been implemented. When I iterated on an AI-implemented feature that was undocumented, it was hard to backtrack on the reasoning behind the code. Not to mention the hassle when picking up a task in a new session! Lastly, if I needed uncommitted, deleted code rewritten, good luck to me. With no artifacts for agents to refer to, consistency AND confidence were hard to achieve.


I was working on multiple prototypes for a specific feature in a complex domain. Changes landed daily, and the feedback was a mix of prototype-specific and feature-specific, so it got messy quickly. I needed a reliable record of why each decision was made, and I didn’t have one. My agents kept revisiting options we had already ruled out. Once I switched to SDD and kept the artifacts up to date, far fewer decisions got lost in history. My agents stopped bringing back options I’d already rejected, and I could explain what changed and why it needed to.


SDD follows the usual pattern of exploring, planning, then implementing. Same fundamentals, but with documentation built in. The spec docs give agents something durable to anchor against. There are several open-source SDD frameworks. I started with spec-kit and later moved to OpenSpec; more on that below.


I like bulleted lists and I hope you do too. Let’s jump into the good and the bad.


### The good


- No re-explaining when I switch agents. I can begin a feature in Codex and continue in Claude Code because both read the same specs. I like picking the agent that suits the work.
- A built-in audit trail. The specs are literally artifacts, so I can see how a feature was developed and why.
- One canonical way of working. AI has a mind of its own, and SDD gives every agent the same guardrails instead of letting each one approach the project differently.


### The bad


- A learning curve. Different tools have different commands and guidelines.
- Drift is on you. Some frameworks are rigid, so iterating on a feature means being deliberate about resolving drift between the codebase and the specs, especially after ad hoc changes.
- The volume of artifacts can feel overwhelming. Engineers aren’t always keen on writing and reading docs (if you are, kudos to you!).


### Battle of the frameworks


If you’re like me, you’re probably asking, “What should I use, and where do I start?” At the end of the day, it comes down to personal preference. The advice that stuck with me during this wave of AI tooling is “use what you are using now until it no longer works for you.” So pick one and experiment until it stops serving you.


I started with[spec-kit](https://speckit.org/) because my colleagues were using it. It’s published by GitHub, which gave it some credibility. After more than five months, I switched to[OpenSpec](https://openspec.dev/) by Fission AI, which I still use today. Here’s how they compared for the way I work:


Table comparing spec-kit and OpenSpec


My trouble with spec-kit was that when I made ad hoc changes and forgot to update its verbose artifacts, the gaps showed up in later iterations. The[converge step](https://github.github.com/spec-kit/reference/agentic-sdd.html) has since been added to spec-kit but OpenSpec’s lightweight, seamless process is hard to move away from.


One thing I enjoyed about spec-kit is its[community marketplace](https://speckit-community.github.io/extensions/) for customizations. If you check it out, you might find some that I created. 👀


### Moving forward


At LeadDev’s[LDX3 conference in New York](https://leaddev.com/leaddev-new-york/) , several talks highlighted SDD, and one piece of advice stuck with me: review the specs first, or better yet, have an agentic reviewer evaluate them. Here’s how I upgraded my workflow after that:


- I write human-readable test cases and keep them in the specs.
- I built a skill that summarizes the spec docs in a voice I can actually follow.
- My code reviewer agent now reviews the specs before it looks at the codebase.
- It also scores how well the specs align with the implementation.
- I run the reviewer before I publish the PR.


That alignment score is how I catch the spec drift I mentioned earlier. It tells me whether the specs I’m reviewing still describe what’s actually implemented.


My flow working with AI has improved with these upgrades. I find it much easier to review a spec doc than an AI-written block of code. Think about it: the point of the artifacts is to explain the change in plain language. Understanding WHY and then WHAT changed has been the most valuable part of my new approach to code reviews.


Having my agents respond in my way of speaking helps too. As many of you have probably noticed, AI agents love to spew a bunch of words that get you lost in the sauce. 🤯 🍝


Running agentic reviewers BEFORE publishing the PR also keeps the review thread short. By the time my PRs go up, there’s usually much less to debate or fix, so they stay clean and straightforward, with no cognitive overload.


### TL;DR


SDD has made me more confident working with AI. Standardized artifacts act as guardrails, so I can move faster without losing clarity, alignment, or accountability; I don’t have to babysit AI to keep it on the right priorities. Yes, there are more docs to keep up with, but I’ll take that over renegotiating with my agents. Once you get the hang of an SDD framework, what looks like upkeep starts to feel like part of the work. 🪄
